I think you really underestimate the powers of rationalization we possess. If there's something we really ought to believe but that conflicts with another belief we cherish or obligates us to do something we don't want to do, then we find it very easy to cook up reasons not to believe that thing.

This started in the very beginning, when the serpent asked Eve, "Has God really said..?"

There's another great example in St. Luke's gospel, when a "rich young ruler" asked Jesus what he needed to do to be saved.

17 As [Jesus] was setting out on a journey, a man ran up to Him and knelt before Him, and asked Him, “Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” 18 And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone. 19 You know the commandments, ‘Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.’” 20 And he said to Him, “Teacher, I have kept all these things from my youth up.” 21 Looking at him, Jesus felt a love for him and said to him, “One thing you lack: go and sell all you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me.” 22 But at these words [a]he was saddened, and he went away grieving, for he was one who owned much property.

The gospel doesn't record what the young man eventually did, but it's easy to imagine that he finally decided to hold onto his wealth by choosing to believe that Jesus wasn't such a great teacher after all. It's a wonderful example of how human beings respond to clear and precise directions that collide with their own self-interest.

If you don't like stuff from the bible, the scientific literature on how we respond to evidence that conflicts with our closely held beliefs is ample. A good modern-day example is climate change. Some people are absolutely masterful at explaining away the evidence, all because a large-scale government response doesn't jibe with their politics, or something like that.
